discovery_and_framing.subtitle: Master the art of scope, geography, and constraints.

lesson.hook: Do not dive into math before you even know what you are counting.
lesson.what: Discovery and framing is the crucial first step of any guesstimate interview. You define the exact geography, timeframe, unit, and inclusions or exclusions.
how: State your exact target metric clearly.
Define the time and place boundaries.
lesson.example: To estimate daily coffee sales in London, I will focus on standard morning commuter takeaway coffees during a typical weekday, excluding evening alcohol sales and rural cafes. This sets a clear baseline before we do any math.
lesson.mistake: Rushing into formulas and calculations without defining boundaries leaves your interviewer completely lost.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the number of commercial flights in the air right now globally.
questions.scenario: You are interviewing at a major travel tech company and need to estimate global flights.
questions.question: What is the best way to handle private jets and military aircraft during your framing?
options: Deliberately exclude them to keep the math manageable.
Add a secret multiplier later in the final calculation.
Include them because they take up actual runway space.
Ask the interviewer if they matter for global traffic.
questions.explanation: Explicitly stating exclusions keeps your model clean and shows strategic discipline. It prevents scope creep from ruining your math later.
whyWrong: Adding secret multipliers hides messy assumptions instead of handling them cleanly upfront in the framework.
A smart candidate might think air traffic includes all planes, but military data is restricted and ruins simple consumer models.
Asking the interviewer shifts ownership away from you, which makes you look weak and unprepared.

questions.caseTitle: Amount of storage required to host all of Spotify's music.
questions.scenario: You are asked to estimate Spotify's total raw audio storage requirements in a system design round.
questions.question: Which scoping choice is most critical for the initial framing step here?
options: Ignore album art and user playlists to focus on audio.
Ask if we should count lossless FLAC files for audiophiles.
Include every single podcast episode ever recorded globally.
Estimate user profile pictures alongside the main catalog.
questions.explanation: Stripping out metadata and non-core files keeps the calculation focused on the main storage driver. This demonstrates strong prioritization skills.
whyWrong: Lossless files are not the standard tier for most users and would distort your average file size baseline.
Podcasts are a massive separate media category that would completely bloat your primary music storage model.
User profile pictures and metadata are tiny rounding errors compared to raw audio files.

questions.caseTitle: How many smartphones are sold in the US annually?
questions.scenario: Your interviewer asks for annual smartphone sales in the United States market today.
questions.question: How should you handle used and refurbished phones in your opening scope?
options: Include them because second hand sales represent real demand.
Count them only if they were traded in at Apple.
Exclude them to focus entirely on new device purchases.
Split them evenly across all major carrier retail stores.
questions.explanation: Market sizing prompts typically target gross new manufacturing shipments and primary retail sales unless specified otherwise. Excluding used phones keeps the primary demand clean.
whyWrong: Splitting them across stores is a calculation tactic, not a discovery and framing decision.
Second hand sales do not generate primary manufacturer revenue in the same way new units do.
Focusing only on Apple trade-ins misses the massive Android secondary market completely.

questions.caseTitle: Amazon.in Daily Sales
questions.scenario: You are estimating daily sales volume for Amazon in the Indian domestic market.
questions.question: What is the best way to treat digital downloads and B2B orders in your frame?
options: Estimate them using gross merchandise value multipliers later.
Deliberately exclude them to keep physical retail grounded.
Ask the interviewer if digital goods matter for revenue.
Include them to capture the full economic marketplace value.
questions.explanation: Bounding your problem to physical goods delivered to households keeps the delivery and order math manageable. B2B and digital goods operate on completely different unit economics.
whyWrong: Using hidden multipliers skips the vital upfront framing step of defining what you count.
Asking the interviewer for permission shows a lack of structured product ownership.
Including digital downloads introduces software margins that break simple physical shipping assumptions.

questions.caseTitle: Saturday Food Delivery Orders in a Large City
questions.scenario: An interviewer asks you to estimate Saturday food delivery orders in a ten million person city.
questions.question: How should you treat grocery deliveries and direct phone orders?
options: Exclude them to focus strictly on app restaurant deliveries.
Ask the panel which delivery apps they personally prefer.
Include them because food delivery covers all food types.
Add them as a separate percentage of total household income.
questions.explanation: Setting clear boundaries ensures you do not mix grocery logistics with hot restaurant meal delivery. Different unit economics require separate mental buckets.
whyWrong: Grocery deliveries happen on completely different schedules and basket sizes than hot meals.
Adding them as an income percentage mixes up demographic segmentation with channel scoping.
Asking about personal preferences wastes precious interview time on irrelevant anecdotes.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the daily revenue of a Starbucks in New York City.
questions.scenario: You need to estimate the daily revenue of a single busy Starbucks location in Manhattan.
questions.question: What is the most professional way to handle airport kiosks and drive-thrus?
options: Include them to capture all possible coffee purchase methods.
Average them out with standard urban store footprints.
Deliberately exclude them because economics differ entirely.
Ask if the manager is running any special holiday promos.
questions.explanation: Manhattan foot traffic operates under vastly different cost and volume structures than highway drive-thrus or airport security zones. Scoping them out preserves model integrity.
whyWrong: Airport kiosks have captive audiences and different pricing, which ruins your baseline assumptions.
Averaging wildly different store formats together produces a meaningless hybrid estimate.
Holiday promotions are temporary operational noise that regular guesstimates ignore.

questions.caseTitle: Bonus: Netflix Monthly Active Users in Brazil
questions.scenario: You are consulting for a streaming service and need to size the Brazilian subscriber base.
questions.question: Which scoping statement demonstrates the best discovery and framing practice?
options: Count active household streaming profiles while excluding free trials.
Estimate mobile data caps before looking at subscriber numbers.
Include every single person living inside the country borders.
Ask the interviewer how many subscribers Netflix currently has.
questions.explanation: Focusing on active paying household profiles filters out inactive accounts and free trials, giving you a realistic base for revenue or engagement models.
whyWrong: Counting every single citizen ignores babies, toddlers, and people without internet access.
Asking for the exact answer defeats the entire purpose of a guesstimate interview case.
Mobile data caps are an implementation detail that belongs deeper in the technical segment.

questions.caseTitle: Bonus: Airbnb Nightly Bookings Worldwide
questions.scenario: You are evaluating travel marketplace metrics and need to size global Airbnb transactions.
questions.question: What is the best way to frame the types of properties included in your count?
options: Add a luxury villa multiplier to your final transaction sum.
Ask the interviewer which countries are currently restricted.
Focus on short-term residential rentals while excluding hotels.
Include traditional hotel rooms since they compete directly.
questions.explanation: Airbnb primarily facilitates peer-to-peer residential stays, so excluding traditional commercial hotels keeps the supply side model aligned with their actual core business.
whyWrong: Luxury multipliers hide sloppy scoping rather than defining what is actually in your market.
Restricted countries are a geography question, whereas properties define the product scope.
Traditional hotels operate on hotel management systems and booking channels outside Airbnb.

structure.subtitle: Master MECE structure to build a clean, calculable estimation tree.

lesson.hook: Stop guessing numbers blindly. Build a tree that does the heavy lifting for you.
lesson.what: Structure means breaking a massive market down into mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive parts. This turns an impossible guess into simple multiplication.
how: Define your scope and explicitly state exclusions.
Split the total market into logical sub-segments.
Check that your branches cover everything without overlap.
lesson.example: For Spotify storage, segment the total catalog size by average song duration and standard audio bitrate. This creates a clear calculation path from tracks to gigabytes.
lesson.mistake: Skipping straight to math without a structured breakdown leaves critical segments uncounted.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the number of commercial flights in the air right now globally.
questions.scenario: You are interviewing at a top tech firm and need to estimate airborne commercial flights globally right now.
questions.question: Which top-down structure best ensures your estimate is mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive?
options: Split global flights by 24 hour time zones and regional flight density.
Calculate total flights using airline revenue and average ticket prices.
Segment by long haul international routes and short haul domestic routes.
Divide by aircraft manufacturer type and average passenger seating capacity.
questions.explanation: Splitting by time zones and regional density captures global activity across a full daily cycle without gaps. Time zones and regional density form a MECE coverage of the globe.
whyWrong: Using revenue and ticket prices relates to financial metrics rather than physical flight counts in the air.
Dividing by route length misses regional and cargo flights that do not fit standard domestic versus international buckets.
A smart candidate might try aircraft types, but manufacturer models do not scale cleanly to global hourly flight counts.

questions.caseTitle: Amount of storage required to host all of Spotify's music.
questions.scenario: An engineering panel asks you to size the raw storage needed to host every single audio track on Spotify.
questions.question: What is the most rigorous structural breakdown for calculating this total audio storage volume?
options: Multiply total tracks by average song duration and standard audio bitrate.
Calculate storage based on active daily users and their playlist downloads.
Estimate total server costs and divide by average gigabyte hosting prices.
Segment songs by music genre and average compression ratios used by artists.
questions.explanation: Multiplying tracks, duration, and bitrate covers every audio file directly through fundamental data units. This creates a calculable tree directly from file characteristics.
whyWrong: User playlist downloads measure consumption rather than the total hosted catalog storage requested by the prompt.
Server costs and hosting prices lead to financial figures instead of raw digital storage capacity.
Genre segmentation is unnecessary and does not cleanly map to standardized file sizes or bitrate calculations.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the global market size for electric scooters.
questions.scenario: You need to size the global market for electric scooters during a product strategy interview case.
questions.question: How should you structure the top-down estimation tree for global electric scooter sales?
options: Calculate market size using average battery life and manufacturing material costs.
Segment by maximum speed capabilities and battery charging station availability.
Divide total sales between consumer retail purchases and commercial fleet rentals.
Split the global population by urban density and personal vehicle adoption rates.
questions.explanation: Splitting between consumer retail and commercial fleets captures all buyers without overlap. Retail and commercial fleet rentals are mutually exclusive channels that cover the whole market.
whyWrong: Battery life and material costs are unit economics details, not top-level market sizing branches.
Speed capabilities and charging stations describe product features rather than total market purchase volume.
Urban density is helpful for context, but population splits alone do not cleanly capture scooter purchase channels.

questions.caseTitle: How many WhatsApp messages are sent worldwide per day?
questions.scenario: An interviewer wants to know the total daily message volume processed by WhatsApp across the globe.
questions.question: Which structural approach provides the cleanest MECE foundation for global message volume?
options: Split messages into text format, photo attachments, and video uploads.
Calculate volume using company server bandwidth and average packet sizes.
Divide total messages by mobile operating systems and cellular network speeds.
Segment active users by demographic regions and average daily message frequency.
questions.explanation: Segmenting users by region and frequency scales message volume cleanly across the global active user base. User regions and frequency form a comprehensive, non overlapping tree.
whyWrong: Splitting by media type leaves out group chat dynamics and fails to cover total volume easily.
Server bandwidth and packet sizes represent technical infrastructure rather than user messaging behavior.
Operating systems and network speeds do not correlate reliably with individual messaging habits.

questions.caseTitle: Number of daily subway riders in Tokyo.
questions.scenario: You are tasked with estimating unique daily subway riders in the Tokyo metropolitan area.
questions.question: What is the best structural way to carve up the Tokyo population for this estimate?
options: Divide residents by age brackets to separate commuter and student travel habits.
Calculate ridership using total station turnstile capacity and train schedules.
Split daily riders by tourist visitors and local corporate office workers.
Segment the population by daily income levels and preferred transit methods.
questions.explanation: Age brackets separate students, working adults, and seniors whose travel habits differ significantly. Demographics by age provide a reliable proxy for daily transit usage rates.
whyWrong: Turnstile capacity and train schedules describe supply constraints rather than actual rider demand.
Tourists and office workers miss large segments of the population including school children and retirees.
Income levels do not dictate subway usage as clearly as age and daily commuting obligations do.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate Google's annual revenue worldwide.
questions.scenario: You are asked to estimate Google annual revenue worldwide during a business case interview.
questions.question: Which structure correctly breaks down Google revenue into distinct, comprehensive pillars?
options: Split revenue streams by geographic regions and local currency exchange rates.
Segment by search ads, YouTube ads, Google Cloud, and app store commissions.
Calculate earnings using global internet users, click-through rates, and ad prices.
Divide total revenue between enterprise software clients and consumer hardware buyers.
questions.explanation: Google makes money through distinct monetization engines that cover its entire business model without overlap. These four pillars represent the true revenue streams of the parent company.
whyWrong: Geographic regions mix different product lines together instead of isolating distinct business models.
Users and click-through rates are calculation inputs for ads, not the top-level revenue pillars.
Enterprise software and consumer hardware ignore the massive advertising engine that drives most of the business.

questions.caseTitle: Netflix Daily Global Streaming Hours
questions.scenario: You need to estimate the total number of hours users spend streaming video on Netflix globally each day.
questions.question: What is the most effective MECE structure to calculate total daily streaming hours?
options: Segment streaming hours by movie length, TV show episodes, and documentaries.
Multiply total paid subscribers by average hours watched per subscriber daily.
Divide global population by broadband internet penetration and subscription tiers.
Calculate total hours using server bandwidth consumption and video bitrates.
questions.explanation: Subscribers multiplied by daily viewing hours per subscriber directly yields total streaming hours. This structure uses the core customer base as the primary calculation node.
whyWrong: Segmenting by content type makes it difficult to estimate aggregate time spent across millions of users.
Broadband penetration and subscription tiers complicate the top level before you account for user habits.
Server bandwidth and bitrates measure data transfer rather than human viewing time.

questions.caseTitle: Duolingo Daily Active Learners
questions.scenario: An interviewer asks you to estimate the number of daily active users learning languages on Duolingo.
questions.question: Which top-down structure creates a solid MECE framework for estimating daily active users?
options: Segment total registered user accounts by geographic region and retention tier.
Divide the global population by smartphone ownership and language learning interest.
Calculate users by daily push notifications sent and average click rates.
Split learners by school students, career professionals, and casual hobbyists.
questions.explanation: Splitting global population by smartphone access and learning interest filters down to the addressable audience. Smartphone ownership and interest form a clean funnel to active users.
whyWrong: Registered accounts often include inactive or churned users, making it a misleading starting point.
Notifications and click rates are product engagement tactics, not population segmentation roots.
Learner intent categories overlap heavily and do not cover the entire active user base cleanly.

assumptions.subtitle: State explicit assumptions with defensible backing rather than guessing blindly.

lesson.hook: Stop pulling numbers out of thin air before interviewers catch you.
lesson.what: Assumptions form the backbone of any top down estimation model. You must state them clearly and back them with logic.
lesson.example: For Spotify, we assume one hundred million tracks and calculate storage based on standard audio bitrates.
lesson.mistake: Picking random numbers without explaining why they make sense for the target market.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the number of commercial flights in the air right now globally.
questions.scenario: You are estimating global commercial flights airborne right this minute.
questions.question: How should you handle private jets and military aircraft in your model?
options: Include them inside a broad aviation growth category
Add a ten percent buffer for private aviation usage
Estimate them separately using military budget data
Deliberately exclude them to keep the math manageable
questions.explanation: Explicitly excluding edge cases keeps your scope clean and manageable. This defensible boundary prevents unnecessary math complexity.
whyWrong: Including them creates unnecessary complexity since their data is hard to source.
Adding arbitrary buffers without clear reasoning violates estimation best practices.
Military data is classified and will derail your core estimation flow.

questions.caseTitle: Amount of storage required to host all of Spotify's music.
questions.scenario: You are calculating the raw storage needed to host all of Spotify's music library.
questions.question: What is the best way to handle user playlists and album art in your setup?
options: Calculate them using average user account storage consumption
Bundle them into a single metadata storage multiplier
Ignore album art and playlists for now to focus on audio
Estimate image file sizes across all active user playlists
questions.explanation: Focusing purely on the core audio files keeps the primary assumption defensible. Secondary assets can be acknowledged and explicitly left out.
whyWrong: User account storage varies wildly and makes your baseline assumption weak.
Multiplying blind metadata figures adds ungrounded complexity to the model.
Calculating image sizes for playlists drags you into unnecessary peripheral math.

questions.caseTitle: How many smartphones are sold in the US annually?
questions.scenario: You are estimating annual smartphone sales in the United States market.
questions.question: How should you treat enterprise bulk orders and used phones?
options: Estimate enterprise sales separately using corporate tech budget reports
Include them to capture the total active device replacement cycle
Add a secondhand market adjustment factor to your total sales
Explicitly exclude them to focus on new consumer purchases
questions.explanation: Explicit exclusions keep your target segment clean and easy to calculate. Trying to blend enterprise and consumer creates messy assumptions.
whyWrong: Corporate tech budgets introduce too many variables for a quick guesstimate.
Mixing enterprise bulk purchases with consumer sales corrupts your adoption math.
Secondhand phones do not count toward new annual hardware sales volume.

questions.caseTitle: Amazon.in Daily Sales
questions.scenario: You are estimating daily sales on Amazon dot in across India.
questions.question: Which assumption should you make regarding digital downloads and B2B orders?
options: Factor in digital downloads using active Prime subscriber penetration rates
Leave them out to keep the physical goods math grounded
Estimate B2B bulk orders using average merchant shipping weights
Include digital goods because they drive high margin platform revenue
questions.explanation: Leaving out non-core items establishes a clear boundary for your physical goods model. This defensible scoping protects your underlying calculations.
whyWrong: Subscriber rates do not cleanly map to digital download transaction counts.
Merchant shipping weights are irrelevant when estimating consumer physical retail volume.
Digital goods follow entirely different logistics and inventory cost structures.

questions.caseTitle: Saturday Food Delivery Orders in a Large City
questions.scenario: You are sizing app-based restaurant deliveries on a Saturday in a large city.
questions.question: How should you treat grocery deliveries and direct phone orders?
options: Explicitly exclude them because habits vary across categories
Combine grocery and food delivery into one massive delivery bucket
Include them since they run on identical third-party logistics networks
Factor them in using standard local restaurant order ratios
questions.explanation: Excluding grocery and phone orders ensures your delivery assumption remains focused. Different categories have different frequency patterns and unit economics.
whyWrong: Combining them destroys the granular accuracy of your top-down model.
Grocery orders and restaurant meals have completely different ordering frequencies.
Local phone orders lack app data transparency and skew delivery averages.

questions.caseTitle: Google Search Queries per Second
questions.scenario: You are calculating global text, image, and voice queries on Google Search.
questions.question: What is the correct approach for handling API traffic and internal pings?
options: Deliberately exclude them to focus on genuine human search behavior
Estimate API traffic using enterprise cloud computing usage benchmarks
Include them because they represent automated queries on the infrastructure
Factor in developer pings as a percentage of total web traffic
questions.explanation: Excluding automated traffic ensures your assumption measures actual user search habits. Human behavior is much easier to segment by population demographics.
whyWrong: Cloud computing benchmarks have no direct correlation to search query frequency.
Automated API calls do not reflect normal daily human search intent.
Developer pings introduce noise that ruins your clean top-down population model.

questions.caseTitle: Netflix Daily Global Streaming Hours
questions.scenario: You are estimating the total daily streaming hours across all Netflix users globally.
questions.question: How should you account for shared accounts and multiple viewers per screen?
options: State an explicit average of viewers per active household login
Assume every single subscriber streams content simultaneously during peak hours
Calculate multi-viewer households using broadband connection speed data reports
Ignore shared accounts because billing tiers already capture household usage
questions.explanation: Stating an explicit average per household grounds your viewing time math in reality. Assuming simultaneous streaming for all users would inflate your numbers.
whyWrong: Assuming everyone streams at once creates an absurdly high and unrealistic volume.
Broadband speeds do not correlate with how many people watch the screen.
Ignoring account sharing misses a major driver of actual viewing hours.

questions.caseTitle: Airbnb Active Listings Worldwide
questions.scenario: You are estimating the total number of active property listings on Airbnb globally.
questions.question: How should you handle vacant homes and inactive host accounts in your model?
options: Estimate inactive hosts using regional real estate vacancy rate statistics
Assume every host lists multiple properties across different urban locations
Define an active listing threshold based on minimum annual bookings
Include all registered properties since they remain visible on the platform
questions.explanation: Defining a clear threshold for activity makes your supply-side assumption defensible. Registered accounts do not equal active marketplace inventory.
whyWrong: Real estate vacancy rates apply to long-term housing, not short-term rentals.
Assuming multiple listings per host without proof skews your supply calculation.
Registered properties often include abandoned accounts that never accept guests.

arithmetic.subtitle: Master the art of clean calculation during high stakes interviews.

lesson.hook: Do not let simple math anxiety ruin a brilliant structured framework.
lesson.what: Arithmetic in guesstimates requires multiplying factors clearly and rounding numbers logically. Clean multiplication steps keep your interviewer following your logic effortlessly.
how: Break complex numbers down into simple multiples.
Round aggressively before multiplying large figures together.
State your intermediate totals aloud to maintain clarity.
lesson.example: If five million people order twice weekly, calculate ten million weekly orders easily.
lesson.mistake: Trying to calculate exact decimals in your head instead of using sensible rounded numbers.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the number of commercial flights in the air right now globally.
questions.scenario: You are calculating global airborne commercial flights across a twenty four hour rolling cycle.
questions.question: If twenty thousand flights fly daily and each stays airborne for three hours, how many are up simultaneously?
options: Two thousand five hundred commercial planes aloft right now.
Two thousand five hundred active flights in total.
Two thousand five hundred commercial airplanes.
Two thousand five hundred planes currently in the sky.
questions.explanation: Divide twenty thousand daily flights by eight three hour blocks to get two thousand five hundred. Clear division makes the math traceable.
whyWrong: A smart candidate might use exact flight hours instead of simple blocks.
Candidates might rush the division step and miss the core calculation.
Someone might forget to mention commercial planes explicitly in the final tally.

questions.caseTitle: Amount of storage required to host all of Spotify's music.
questions.scenario: You are sizing the raw audio storage for one hundred million tracks on Spotify.
questions.question: With one hundred million tracks averaging four minutes at one megabyte per minute, what is the total storage?
options: Four hundred thousand gigabytes required for tracks.
Four hundred thousand gigabytes of raw audio storage space.
Four hundred thousand gigabytes.
Four hundred thousand gigabytes of total audio data.
questions.explanation: One hundred million tracks multiplied by four megabytes each equals four hundred million megabytes, which converts to four hundred thousand gigabytes.
whyWrong: A smart person might include album art storage by accident in this number.
A candidate might mistakenly convert megabytes straight to gigabytes by dividing by one thousand.
Someone could confuse megabytes with kilobytes during the initial track sizing estimation.

questions.caseTitle: How many smartphones are sold in the US annually?
questions.scenario: You are estimating annual smartphone sales in the United States for a consumer electronics market sizing case.
questions.question: If three hundred thirty million people buy a new phone every three years, what is the annual sales volume?
options: One hundred ten million smartphones sold each year.
One hundred ten million new smartphones sold annually.
One hundred ten million devices purchased every year.
One hundred ten million phones.
questions.explanation: Divide the three hundred thirty million population by the three year replacement cycle to get one hundred ten million annual sales.
whyWrong: Someone could use a four year replacement cycle by mistake in the calculation.
A smart candidate might multiply population by three instead of dividing by three.
A candidate might factor in enterprise bulk purchases incorrectly into consumer sales.

questions.caseTitle: Amazon.in Daily Sales
questions.scenario: You are calculating daily physical goods orders on Amazon in India for a market sizing exercise.
questions.question: If three hundred million households order one package every ten days, what is the daily order volume?
options: Thirty million daily orders.
Thirty million daily package deliveries processed across India.
Thirty million orders fulfilled every day.
Thirty million packages delivered to households daily.
questions.explanation: Divide three hundred million households by the ten day frequency to arrive at thirty million daily orders.
whyWrong: A candidate might accidentally multiply households by ten instead of dividing.
A smart person might confuse household counts with total individual population figures.
Someone could use a seven day weekly cycle by mistake in the math.

questions.caseTitle: Uber Rides Worldwide in a Day
questions.scenario: You are estimating global daily rides for Uber across ten thousand cities worldwide.
questions.question: If ten thousand cities average two thousand rides per city daily, what is the global daily total?
options: Twenty million rides across all cities.
Twenty million trips taken worldwide every day.
Twenty million rides.
Twenty million daily rides completed globally.
questions.explanation: Multiply ten thousand cities by two thousand rides each to get twenty million daily rides worldwide.
whyWrong: A smart person might add instead of multiplying the two figures together.
Someone could assume every city has identical ride volume without segmenting tiers.
A candidate might miscount zeros when multiplying thousands by thousands.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the daily revenue of a Starbucks in New York City.
questions.scenario: You are breaking down the daily revenue of a busy Manhattan Starbucks location across operating shifts.
questions.question: If three hundred morning customers spend ten dollars each, what is the morning rush revenue total?
options: Three thousand dollars from morning coffee sales.
Three thousand dollars in morning revenue.
Three thousand dollars earned during morning peak.
Three thousand dollars.
questions.explanation: Multiply three hundred customers by ten dollars average ticket size to get three thousand dollars in revenue.
whyWrong: A smart person might include afternoon mobile orders in the morning block.
A candidate might divide instead of multiplying the customer count and ticket size.
Someone could use a twenty dollar ticket size by overestimating pastry purchases.

questions.caseTitle: Netflix Global Annual Subscription Revenue
questions.scenario: You are estimating global subscription revenue for Netflix using a top down subscriber tier model.
questions.question: If two hundred million subscribers pay an average of fifteen dollars monthly, what is the annual revenue?
options: Thirty six billion dollars in total yearly subscription revenue.
Thirty six billion dollars collected annually from global streaming users.
Thirty six billion dollars generated by Netflix each year.
Thirty six billion dollars.
questions.explanation: Two hundred million times fifteen dollars is three billion monthly, multiplied by twelve months gives thirty six billion dollars annually.
whyWrong: A candidate might forget to multiply the monthly total by twelve months.
Someone could use a ten dollar average price point by assuming lower emerging market tiers.
A smart person might include advertising revenue tiers incorrectly in basic subscription math.

questions.caseTitle: Spotify Premium Family Plan Conversion
questions.scenario: You are calculating monthly revenue for Spotify family plan upgrades in a European market case.
questions.question: If five million users upgrade to a fifteen dollar family plan, what is the total monthly revenue?
options: Seventy five million dollars generated every month.
Seventy five million dollars.
Seventy five million dollars collected from upgrades.
Seventy five million dollars in monthly subscription revenue.
questions.explanation: Multiply five million users by fifteen dollars each to calculate seventy five million dollars in monthly revenue.
whyWrong: Someone could use a ten dollar individual price point by mixing up plan tiers.
A smart person might calculate annual revenue instead of the requested monthly figure.
A candidate might divide the user count by the price instead of multiplying.

sanity_check.subtitle: Reality check your final number against known reference points.

lesson.hook: Stop trusting your math blindly before the interviewer laughs at your billions.
lesson.what: A sanity check is a quick reality test of your final number against known real world benchmarks. It ensures your calculations did not accidentally produce an impossible scale.
how: Identify a known benchmark metric for comparison.
Compare your total output per capita or per day.
Adjust your underlying assumptions if the math defies logic.
lesson.example: If your model says a coffee shop serves fifty thousand coffees daily, pause and check if the staff can physically pour one per second.
lesson.mistake: Accepting a wildly impossible final number just because you multiplied the factors correctly.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the number of commercial flights in the air right now globally.
questions.scenario: You just calculated twenty five thousand planes airborne right now.
questions.question: How do you perform a proper sanity check on this global total?
options: Compare against total daily flights tracked by major aviation databases.
Verify the total passenger capacity matches global hotel room counts.
Check if each airline has enough pilots to fly them.
Assume the math is correct because multiplication was done cleanly.
questions.explanation: Comparing your output against published aviation industry flight statistics is the most direct validation. It anchors your abstract calculation in concrete reality.
whyWrong: Hotel room counts measure accommodation rather than active commercial aviation traffic volume.
Pilot availability is an operational constraint rather than a direct check on total aircraft currently aloft.
Trusting unchecked multiplication defeats the entire purpose of doing a structured sanity check.

questions.caseTitle: Amount of storage required to host all of Spotify's music.
questions.scenario: Your model outputs one hundred petabytes of total audio storage for Spotify.
questions.question: What is the best way to sanity check this storage calculation?
options: Ensure users have enough phone storage to download every song.
Compare the total storage against known public data center capacities.
Multiply average track size by total catalog size to verify baseline.
Check how many physical hard drives fit inside a server rack.
questions.explanation: Comparing your derived storage size against known public benchmarks for large streaming services grounds your numbers. It catches massive order of magnitude errors instantly.
whyWrong: User device storage limits have little correlation with total server side music hosting requirements.
Multiplying track size by catalog size is how you built the model, not a sanity check.
Hard drive physical rack sizing is an infrastructure detail unrelated to high level storage validation.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the daily revenue of a Starbucks in New York City.
questions.scenario: Your model concludes a single Manhattan Starbucks makes fifty thousand dollars daily.
questions.question: How should you sanity check this daily revenue figure?
options: Verify that rental costs in Manhattan match the projected profit margin.
Calculate if a barista can process enough transactions within operating hours.
Check if total neighborhood coffee consumption supports this large store revenue.
Assume high foot traffic justifies any revenue number you calculate.
questions.explanation: Checking transaction throughput against physical time limits and staffing constraints reveals if the revenue is logistically possible. Fifty thousand dollars requires processing hundreds of orders every single hour.
whyWrong: Rental costs and profit margins are financial variables distinct from transaction volume throughput.
Neighborhood coffee consumption is already part of your initial top down demand estimation.
Assuming high traffic justifies any number skips the actual validation process entirely.

questions.caseTitle: How many WhatsApp messages are sent worldwide per day?
questions.scenario: You calculate one hundred billion messages sent globally every single day.
questions.question: What is a reliable way to sanity check this messaging volume?
options: Verify that smartphone batteries can sustain this heavy messaging activity level.
Compare daily message volume against total global smartphone user population counts.
Ensure cellular networks have enough bandwidth to transmit all data packets.
Calculate average messages per user to see if humanly possible.
questions.explanation: Breaking the total down to a per user basis lets you evaluate if thirty messages per person daily makes sense. It prevents you from pitching absurdly high or low daily totals.
whyWrong: Battery consumption limits do not provide a clear numerical benchmark for daily message volume.
Comparing against population counts gives total users, but does not test per person messaging frequency.
Cellular network bandwidth is an infrastructure concern rather than a personal usage behavior check.

questions.caseTitle: How many tennis balls can fit in a Boeing 747?
questions.scenario: Your calculation says two million tennis balls fit inside the aircraft cabin.
questions.question: How do you sanity check this physical volume estimation?
options: Assume the packing efficiency percentage accurately accounts for empty cabin spaces.
Compare total ball volume against known cargo capacity limits in liters.
Measure the exact diameter of a standard tennis ball with precision.
Check if the aircraft wings can support the weight of tennis balls.
questions.explanation: Checking your calculated volume against official aircraft cargo capacity in cubic meters or liters instantly exposes math errors. It keeps your spatial estimation grounded in real aircraft dimensions.
whyWrong: Assuming packing efficiency is correct ignores the need to validate the final output against benchmarks.
Measuring a single ball precision is a setup step, not a macro level sanity check.
Wing support is a structural weight question, whereas fitting balls is primarily a volume capacity test.

questions.caseTitle: Number of daily subway riders in Tokyo.
questions.scenario: Your model yields twenty five million daily subway riders in Tokyo.
questions.question: What is the most effective sanity check for this transit number?
options: Verify that platform safety barriers can withstand massive crowd pressures.
Ensure train schedules run on time during the morning rush hour.
Compare your rider count against the total Tokyo metro population size.
Calculate the total electricity needed to power all station ticket gates.
questions.explanation: Comparing daily ridership against total population helps you realize twenty five million riders exceeds the entire city population. That simple comparison flags an obvious overcount.
whyWrong: Platform safety barriers are physical safety features rather than a ridership volume benchmark.
Train schedule punctuality is an operational metric unrelated to passenger count validation.
Electricity needs for ticket gates do not help validate passenger trip volume totals.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate Netflix global monthly active subscribers
questions.scenario: You calculate four billion active Netflix subscribers globally across all regions.
questions.question: How do you perform a quick sanity check on this subscriber total?
options: Check if production studios can produce enough shows for everyone.
Assume global smartphone penetration supports high streaming service adoption rates.
Verify that video streaming bandwidth costs match company profit margins.
Compare your total against the global broadband internet connected population.
questions.explanation: Comparing subscriber totals against the worldwide broadband internet population immediately reveals that four billion exceeds the total number of connected households globally.
whyWrong: Studio production capacity is an operational input rather than a subscriber volume validation check.
Smartphone penetration is too broad since streaming primarily happens on TVs and broadband homes.
Bandwidth costs and profit margins are financial figures rather than direct subscriber base checks.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate annual global sales of Apple iPhones
questions.scenario: Your top down model estimates one billion iPhones sold annually worldwide.
questions.question: What is the best sanity check for this annual hardware sales figure?
options: Verify that retail store employees can process transactions fast enough.
Check if mobile network carriers have enough data plans available.
Calculate average manufacturing assembly time for a single device unit.
Compare the final units against total global smartphone shipments.
questions.explanation: Checking your annual sales total against published global smartphone shipment data provides an immediate reality check. It ensures your model aligns with known industry analyst reports.
whyWrong: Retail store processing speed does not account for online purchases and carrier stores.
Network data plan availability is largely independent of annual hardware purchase volumes.
Assembly time is a micro manufacturing detail rather than a macro market sales validation.

sensitivity.subtitle: Master the art of checking your assumptions under pressure.

lesson.hook: Knowing your math is useless if your core assumption is off by a mile.
lesson.what: Sensitivity analysis identifies which single variable moves your final output the most. It tells you where to focus your mental energy when time is running out.
how: Find the variable with the highest multiplicative leverage.
Calculate the percentage shift when that single input alters.
State clearly which assumption breaks your model if wrong.
lesson.example: For Spotify storage, your math is most sensitive to the average bit rate per track. If compression changes, the entire total shifts dramatically.
lesson.mistake: Testing minor variables like metadata size instead of the core traffic driver.

questions.caseTitle: Amount of storage required to host all of Spotify's music.
questions.scenario: You are estimating the total raw storage needed for all tracks on Spotify globally.
questions.question: Which assumption is the final storage calculation most sensitive to?
options: The average file size of a standard audio track.
The metadata storage required for user playlists.
The total number of active users streaming daily.
The distribution of genres across independent artists.
questions.explanation: Audio file size directly multiplies the entire catalog count, making it the primary leverage point. Small changes here swing petabytes of data.
whyWrong: Metadata is tiny compared to raw audio files and will not move the total storage needle significantly.
Active users matter for bandwidth but do not directly change the raw storage footprint of the music catalog.
Genre distribution has a negligible impact on the overall average bit rate and file size math.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the daily revenue of a Starbucks in New York City.
questions.scenario: You are calculating daily revenue for a flagship Manhattan Starbucks location on a Tuesday.
questions.question: Which variable will cause the largest shift in total revenue if your estimate is wrong?
options: The cost of dairy milk substitutes purchased weekly.
The percentage of customers who buy a pastry item.
The average price paid per transaction.
The total number of customers served during peak morning hours.
questions.explanation: Morning peak volume drives the vast majority of daily transactions in an urban commuter store. Missing this flow ruins the entire revenue model.
whyWrong: COGS affects profit margins rather than the top line revenue calculation you are trying to estimate.
Food attach rates matter, but beverage volume remains the core engine of daily store earnings.
Average ticket size stays relatively stable due to standard pricing, making volume the higher leverage swing factor.

questions.caseTitle: Google Search Queries per Second
questions.scenario: You are estimating global Google search volume over a standard twenty four hour cycle.
questions.question: How does your final queries per second number move if internet penetration in developing regions is overestimated?
options: The monetization rate per query improves across western markets.
The average search query length increases due to language barriers.
The server latency for image searches decreases globally.
The total query volume drops significantly across all time zones.
questions.explanation: Overestimating user population in developing regions inflates the base multiplier, so correcting it drops total global volume. This variable controls the entire scale of the model.
whyWrong: Ad monetization rates are separate from raw search query volume calculations in a top down model.
Population counts affect total query volume rather than the linguistic length of individual text searches.
Infrastructure latency is a technical engineering metric unrelated to population size assumptions.

questions.caseTitle: How many ride hailing drivers are active in a large city now?
questions.scenario: You are sizing active ride hailing drivers in a five million person city during peak afternoon hours.
questions.question: What happens to your driver count if you assume drivers work full shifts instead of part time splits?
options: The commission fee charged by the platform goes up.
Your total active driver count becomes drastically underestimated.
The total city population required for the model decreases.
The average trip distance for passengers increases substantially.
questions.explanation: Part time shift splitting means more unique human drivers log in during peak hours, so ignoring it leads to a severe undercount. This is the most sensitive behavioral assumption in the case.
whyWrong: Platform commission rates are set by business policy rather than individual driver shift patterns.
City population is a fixed demographic input that does not move based on driver shift schedules.
Driver shift lengths do not physically change how far passengers travel across the city grid.

questions.caseTitle: Estimate the global market size for electric scooters.
questions.scenario: You are building a top down model for the global annual sales of urban electric kick scooters.
questions.question: Which assumption carries the highest sensitivity risk for your total market size calculation?
options: The annual replacement rate of commuter scooters.
The average wattage of the electric motor inside.
The typical color preference of urban riders.
The shipping cost from manufacturing plants in Asia.
questions.explanation: Replacement frequency multiplies the active installed base to determine annual sales volume. Getting this lifecycle number wrong skews the final market size by billions.
whyWrong: Motor wattage varies by model tier but has minimal impact on total unit sales volume estimations.
Aesthetic choices like color do not alter the macro purchasing behavior or total market demand.
Logistics costs affect unit economics and retail pricing rather than total unit sales volume.

questions.caseTitle: Number of daily subway riders in Tokyo.
questions.scenario: You are estimating daily unique subway riders in the Tokyo metropolitan area on a weekday.
questions.question: Which variable will distort your final rider count the most if your initial estimate is flawed?
options: The average ticket price for a single zone ride.
The percentage of commuters who transfer between different subway lines.
The cleaning schedule of platform floors during off peak hours.
The total number of vending machines located inside stations.
questions.explanation: Transfer rates determine whether multi line journeys count as single riders or multiple trips. Misjudging this directly distorts the unique daily passenger total.
whyWrong: Ticket pricing affects revenue calculations rather than the physical count of human passenger trips.
Cleaning schedules are operational logistics that do not influence passenger journey counts.
Station vending is an ancillary retail revenue stream unrelated to commuter ridership volume.

questions.caseTitle: Netflix Daily Global Streaming Hours
questions.scenario: You are estimating total hours streamed on Netflix worldwide on a typical Sunday evening.
questions.question: Which core assumption dictates the sensitivity of your total streaming hours calculation?
options: The subscription tier distribution across standard and premium plans.
The number of original movies released by the platform monthly.
The percentage of users streaming on mobile devices versus TVs.
The average duration of content watched per active subscriber session.
questions.explanation: Session duration directly multiplies the user base to yield total hours. If session length is off by thirty minutes, billions of streaming hours vanish from the model.
whyWrong: Tier distribution affects billing revenue rather than the total volume of hours consumed.
Content release cadence influences subscriber acquisition rather than daily streaming duration.
Device type changes video resolution and bandwidth but has a minor effect on total watch time.

questions.caseTitle: Apple App Store Daily Downloads
questions.scenario: You are estimating total daily app downloads across the global iOS App Store ecosystem.
questions.question: How does your sensitivity model react if smartphone upgrade cycles lengthen globally?
options: New device activation volume drops, reducing initial app download spikes.
The average file size of downloaded mobile applications increases rapidly.
The developer commission split enforced by the platform goes down.
The proportion of paid apps versus free downloads shifts dramatically.
questions.explanation: Longer phone lifecycles mean fewer new device setups, which is the primary driver of bulk app downloads. This structural shift moves the entire daily download baseline.
whyWrong: Hardware upgrade cycles are entirely separate from software application file size metrics.
Platform commission splits are determined by corporate policy rather than consumer hardware trends.
Monetization pricing models depend on developer strategy rather than hardware replacement timing.
